newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel plans to pump fresh aid to settlements.
newsitem.headline: Israel plans to pump fresh aid to settlements.

text.p: Israel plans to pump some $16.5 million into further development of Jewish settlements, the treasury said on Wednesday, but the step may spark unrest within Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's ruling coalition.

"We are transferring 56 million shekels to the settlements, as part of the government's decision some time ago to grant favoured development status to these areas," Treasury spokesman Eli Yosef told Reuters.

The settlement issue is at the heart of a severe crisis in Israeli-PLO peace talks, which broke down in March after Netanyahu's cabinet sent bulldozers to break ground on a new Jewish enclave in East Jerusalem.

Treasury sources said the transfer, redirecting funds originally allocated for projects within Israel, formally required approval by parliament's finance committee. But the sources said the funds had already been transferred.

The step drew immediate opposition from lawmakers -- among them key supporters of the Netanyahu government -- who noted that cuts in budget allocations to the needy in Israel would fund much of the new spending in the West Bank and Gaza.
Netanyahu rode to an upset victory a year ago, promising voters in disadvantaged areas who supported him that their backing for settlements would not drain funds from their neighbourhoods.
Finance Committee Chairman Maxim Levy, a leader of the Gesher party, a key coalition partner, strongly criticised the plan as "chutzpah (shameless audacity) of the first order."

The funding plan would cut by 15 percent the budget for housing immigrants and welfare recipients, and by 10 percent the budgets for developing poor neighbourhoods and Arab Israeli population centres, parliamentary sources said.
It follows attempts by Washington, Israel's main benefactor and co-sponsor of the derailed talks, to convince the Jewish state to curb settlement work to jumpstart peace negotiations.
"Not only will the weakest become even more needy, but (the plan) could bring about the collapse of the peace process," said Abraham Shohat, former Labour finance minister.
Palestinians have demanded Israel freeze new settlement work if the talks are to continue.

Further spurring Palestinian ire, Israeli crews began tearing down an Arab house in East Jerusalem on Wednesday, less than 24 hours after a Sinai desert summit in which Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and Netanyahu met to seek ways to resuscitate the talks.
An Israeli court ordered the work stopped in mid-demolition, pending a hearing.

Israel occupied East Jerusalem in 1967 and claimed the whole city as its capital. The claim is not recognised internationally. Palestinians want the city's eastern sector as the capital of their future state.
Last August, the Netanyahu government rescinded a partial freeze on settlement decreed by the previous Labour government.
The right-religious coalition later declared West Bank and Gaza settlement areas "A", or most-favoured development zones, a designation usually reserved for poor towns inside Israel.
Levy said his committee would try to block the funding plan, and that he would bring the issue before parliament for debate.

Even a settler leader slammed the plan as discriminating against the needy. "The poor neighbourhoods, the weak, the immigrants need the money no less than the settlements, said finance committee member Zvi Hendel, a Gaza settler chief.
"There are enough inflated budget clauses from which the money could come, without doing this in an impudent manner, drawing opposition from the Israeli people. ($1=3.38 shekels)
